title: Six Chennai Restaurants Keeping Karnataka's Tiffin Tradition Alive
excerpt: From Woodlands' legendary rava idli to Tiffin Shastra's Darshini-style service, the city's vegetarian scene draws deeply from its cross-border culinary roots.
body:
• Chennai's vegetarian dining scene is experiencing a boom in Karnataka-style tiffin, with benne dose, thatte idli, and Mangalore buns joining the city's already rich South Indian repertoire.
  • The trend traces back to the 1930s, when restaurateurs from villages near Mangalore and Udupi set up iconic establishments like Dasaprakash and Woodlands in Chennai.
  • Six restaurants — from heritage institutions to modern Darshini-style chains — offer standout Karnataka vegetarian food across the city.
  • Woodlands' Krishna restaurant is credited with introducing the masala dosa to Chennai, while Eating Circles pioneered Bengaluru's sweet sambar in the city nearly a decade ago.

A Cross-Border Culinary Bond

The crispy, butter-soaked benne dose has become one of India's defining vegetarian food trends of the 2020s. But Chennai's appetite for Karnataka cuisine is nothing new. The city's 'Udupi hotels' began appearing as early as the 1930s, when conscientious restaurateurs from small villages near Mangalore and Udupi migrated to set up what would become institutions. Dasaprakash and Woodlands were among the first, and it was Woodlands that is believed to have introduced the masala dosa to Chennai.

The latest wave, driven by the popularity of benne dose, thatte idli, and Mangalore buns, has added a new generation of restaurants to this legacy. Here are six places keeping Karnataka's tiffin tradition alive in Chennai.

Krishna Restaurant, New Woodlands Hotel

The flagship of Udupi cuisine in Chennai, Krishna has been the standard-bearer for decades. The restaurant comes alive during 'tiffin' time — that extended window between lunch and dinner. Its rava idli, a dish invented in a Bengaluru restaurant, is arguably Chennai's best. The original masala dosa and Mangalore bondas are crowd favorites, and the filter coffee is consistently excellent.

Where: Dr Radhakrishnan Salai, Mylapore

Eating Circles

Nearly a decade ago, Eating Circles introduced Chennai to Bengaluru-style snacks with its open-style masala dosa and a distinctive sweet sambar made with jaggery. Beyond dosas, the Maddur Vade — a crunchy creation made with rice flour, maida, rava, and generous onions and groundnuts — is worth ordering. Wash it down with the restaurant's signature rose milk or filter coffee.

Where: CP Ramasamy Road, Alwarpet

Sashwatha Café

This energetic restaurant debuted on Chamiers Road before expanding to Anna Nagar. Contemporary interiors frame a menu focused squarely on Karnataka-style tiffin. The open benne dosa and Mysore masala dosa are the stars. Don't skip the akki roti or the rose kesari bath.

Where: Chamiers Road, Nandanam

Mathsya at Udupi Home

Housed within a budget hotel with roots stretching back to 1932, Mathsya serves authentic Udupi cuisine that feels unchanged by time. The Mysore masala dosa comes with its trademark paste, and the bite-sized Mangalore bonda is a reliable choice. The neer dosa — rice-flour crepes paired with jaggery and grated coconut — is light and elegant. For the full experience, order the special Udupi platter.

Where: Halls Road, Egmore

Upavihar

Now a chain with multiple locations, Upavihar has built a loyal base for what it calls 'Tasty Thindi' — Kannada for food or snack. Like its peers, dosas are the biggest draw, but regulars also swear by the khara bath and filter coffee.

Where: East Coast Road, Injambakkam

Tiffin Shastra

Bengaluru's beloved Darshini-style restaurants — self-service, stand-up counters, quick service — have found a Chennai outpost in Tiffin Shastra. The menu blends Bengaluru and Chennai breakfast traditions, offering everything from ghee pongal and Mangalore buns to bun butter jam and dosa.

Where: Second Avenue, 11th Main Road, Anna Nagar West
